title: 29. Observability & Operational Signals
content:
# 29. Observability & Operational Signals

Observability is the practice of understanding a system from the signals it emits. From the CLI, the main signals are logs, metrics, traces, health checks, process state, and kernel messages.

## Learning goals

By the end of this module, you should be able to:

- collect useful evidence from logs, metrics, and host state;
- distinguish symptoms from causes;
- use time windows and correlation IDs;
- build simple health and smoke checks;
- avoid noisy checks that hide real failures.

## Logs

```bash
journalctl -u api.service --since "30 minutes ago"
journalctl -p warning..alert --since today
```

Good log review starts with a time window and a question. Look for first error, repeated error, change in rate, and messages around restarts.

## Metrics from the host

```bash
uptime
free -h
df -h
ss -s
ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head
```

These are not a full metrics system, but they quickly show resource pressure during an incident. Capture values before and after a change.

## Health checks

A health check should test something meaningful and return a clear status:

```bash
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/health
```

`curl -f` treats HTTP error status as failure, `-sS` keeps output quiet while still showing errors. For user-facing verification, test through the same path users use, not only localhost.

## Traces and correlation

If an application emits request IDs or trace IDs, preserve them in incident notes:

```bash
journalctl -u api.service --since "10 minutes ago" | grep 'request_id=abc123'
```

Correlation beats guessing. One request followed across proxy, app, and database logs is often more useful than thousands of unrelated lines.

## Kernel and platform signals

```bash
dmesg -T | tail -n 100
journalctl -k --since "1 hour ago"
```

OOM kills, disk errors, network driver messages, and filesystem problems may only appear in kernel logs.

## Alert quality

A good alert has an owner, threshold, duration, impact, and runbook. A bad alert fires frequently without action. From the CLI, validate whether an alert matches current reality before acting.

## Simple smoke scripts

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u

curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/health >/dev/null
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/version
```

Smoke checks should be fast, deterministic, and safe to run repeatedly.

## Practice

For a local service, write an observation report with current health status, recent warnings/errors, CPU and memory state, disk state, listening ports, and one user-facing smoke test. Include exact commands and timestamps.
